extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (prosecutors/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification supports claimed subject matter under the written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph), including examiner burdens, common circumstances where issues arise, treatment of new matter, and permissible/amendment practices. Primarily for use in prosecution, priority claims, interferences, and reissue review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment affecting a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to the claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed. An amendment to the specification (e.g., a change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case citation: In re Wright, 866 F.2d 422. Examiner must ensure any claim amendment is supported by originally filed disclosure; look for explicit, implicit, or inherent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on filing date of parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier filed U.S. application if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, in the earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Scheiber. Examiner must determine whether earlier application discloses claimed subject matter with adequate written description for priority entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or the filing date of a provisional application only if the corresponding foreign or provisional application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli. Evaluate foreign/provisional disclosures for written description support before granting priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; earlier applications relied upon for benefit must likewise meet 112 requirements for the subject matter of the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Fields v. Conover (broad generic disclosure insufficient for a specific compound); Hyatt v. Boone. When interference benefit is claimed, ensure earlier app meets written description for the count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner regarding the written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless and until sufficient evidence or reasoning rebuts the presumption. The examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: In re Wertheim; In re Marzocchi. Examiner must establish factual findings and reasonable rationale; mere conclusory statements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements (what to include in a written-description rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the conclusion, including (A) identification of the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establishment of a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at filing would not recognize that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general allegation of unpredictability is insufficient. A simple statement pointing out where support is lacking may suffice for new/amended claims. Cite Hyatt v. Dudas; suggest claim amendments where appropriate, mindful of prohibition on adding new matter (see Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to applicant’s reply when faced with a written-description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, before repeating any 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 rejection, the examiner must review the record as a whole (including amendments, arguments, and evidence). If the record now demonstrates adequacy, do not repeat the rejection; if not, fully respond to rebuttal arguments and properly address any further showings (e.g., affidavits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Alton. When maintaining rejection, thoroughly analyze and discuss affidavits and any new evidence submitted by applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to the scope of claims must be supported by original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2163. Applies to broadenings, narrowings, numerical range changes, and terminology changes; examine original disclosure for express/implicit/inherent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claim — omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element the applicant described as essential/critical does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Gentry Gallery v. Berkline; Johnson Worldwide v. Zebco; Tronzo v. Biomet; In re Wilder. If specification describes a feature as 'the only possible location' or 'essential,' omission will likely fail. Compare In re Peters where a limitation was nonessential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of a generic claim (genus supported by species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genus claim may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species; a single species supports a genus only when disclosure indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. If the genus exhibits substantial variation, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis; In re Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe; Tronzo; In re Gosteli. Examine whether the disclosed species are 'representative' and whether operability across genus would be predicted by ordinary artisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim (introducing unsupported limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Subgeneric recitations may or may not be acceptable depending on factual communication to skilled artisans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Fujikawa v. Wattanasin; In re Ruschig; Ex parte Ohshiro; In re Lukach; Ex parte Sorenson; In re Smith; In re Wilder. 'Laundry list' disclosures are insufficient to reasonably lead to every species; decide each case on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations (changing numerical ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical ranges, determine which ranges a skilled artisan would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure. Some range modifications (e.g., adding open-ended 'at least' without upper limit) can extend beyond original disclosure and fail the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: In re Wertheim (example where 'at least 35%' without upper limit failed but 'between 35% and 60%' met requirement); Purdue Pharma v. Faulding; Union Oil v. Atlantic Richfield. Consider original described ranges and specific examples to assess support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of written description generally arises with respect to claim subject matter. If applicant amends or attempts to amend abstract, specification or drawings to add content not described in the application as filed, new matter issues arise. Information present in any one part of the original application may be added to any other part without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory prohibitions: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no new matter in pending application) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue). If added content is not in original filing, treat as new matter and object/reject as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter (examiner actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure (abstract, specification, drawings), the examiner should object to the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter. If new matter is added to claims, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph - written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Rasmussen. Examiner should still consider subject matter added to claims when making prior art rejections since applicant may overcome the new matter rejection. If specification amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, reject the claims under 112 para. 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of new matter objections and/or rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection of claims for new matter is reviewable by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (BPAI), whereas an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181. If both claims and specification contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and objection, the issue is appealable and should not be decided by petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate procedural route depending on whether action is an objection (petitionable) or rejection (appealable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter not disclosed in remainder of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an originally filed claim discloses material not disclosed elsewhere in the specification, applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Benno. Use Form Paragraph 7.44 when originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis (see MPEP §608.01(o)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application which are supported in the original description do NOT constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle when rephrasing or correcting specification language so long as the same meaning is maintained and support exists in the originally filed disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing (mere rewording)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage that preserves the same meaning does not constitute new matter; inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing is not new matter. However, if multiple definitions exist for a term, adding a particular definition must be clearly supported by the original filing to avoid new matter/lack of written description issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Anderson; Scarring Corp. v. Megan (substitution of a more specific term was permissible where original disclosure intended that meaning). Be cautious adding definitions that narrow or change meaning unless support is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious errors (corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Odd. However, applicant may not rely on foreign priority documents to support correction of an error in the U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. For certain filing situations (e.g., inadvertent omission for applications filed on/after Sept. 21, 2004), 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.57 may apply (see MPEP §201.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function, theory, or advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent application discloses a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, or operates according to a theory or has an advantage, the application necessarily discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not explicitly stated; the application may later be amended to recite it without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: In re Reynolds; In re Smythe; In re Robertson (inherency requires extrinsic evidence making clear the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and recognizable by persons of ordinary skill; cannot be established by mere probabilities or possibilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may incorporate material from another document by reference; information incorporated is as much a part of the application as if the text were repeated in the application, and replacing incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP §608.01(p) for Office policy on incorporation by reference. Treat incorporated material as part of the application as filed for written description/new matter analyses.
